power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: When One Random Effect Is Not Enough: Mixture Model Meta-Analysis

text.text: Handling between-study differences in effect sizes, or heterogeneity, is a key challenge in meta-analysis.

The common assumption that heterogeneity is normally distributed implies an absence of systematic sources of heterogeneity, or known and measured sources of heterogeneity that can be controlled using moderator analysis.

These assumptions fall short when effect sizes originate from multiple unknown subpopulations -for example, due to different research traditions, unmeasured moderators, publication bias, and outliers.

It has been argued that finite mixture models -also known as latent class analysis (LCA) -can capture these unobserved subgroups, but there is currently no generalized framework for estimating such models.
We introduce open source software for estimating random-effects mixture, or "remix" meta-analyses.
Implemented in OpenMx, these structural equation models can be fully customized and further extended.

We conducted a simulation study to evaluate the remix algorithm's convergence, bias and confidence interval coverage, and the performance of several class enumeration metrics: the AIC, BIC, and ICL information criteria, predictive model comparison (PMC), and cross-validation.
Results show that the method is fast and has low bias, but confidence interval coverage is below nominal levels, and class enumeration remains challenging -which are known limitations of LCA.
Nevertheless, remix meta-analysis is the appropriate method when effect sizes originate from a mixture of unobserved subpopulations; a scenario which is arguably commonplace in meta-analysis.

When One Random Effect Is Not Enough: Mixture Model Meta-Analysis When synthesizing effect sizes originating from different studies, a key question is how to properly account for between-study differences.
The choice of an appropriate statistical model depends on theoretical assumptions about the sources of heterogeneity.
For example, the fixed-effect model assumes no differences in true effect size.

If effect sizes result from close replications of a particular experiment, it is sensible to assume one true population effect, which implies that any differences between observed effect sizes must be due to sampling error.

If effect sizes instead originate from a wide range of different studies, conducted in different labs with unique designs and distinct measures -then we might expert there to be variance in true effect sizes.
If we assume that there are no systematic differences, then the random effects model can estimate the variance of true effect sizes, τ² .

If we know that there are systematic sources of heterogeneity, for example, because some studies used a stronger manipulation than others, and we have coded these sources as moderator variables, then we can control for these differences using meta-regression.

And finally, if we suspect that there are systematic sources of heterogeneity, but we don't know which moderator variables are relevant, machine learning methods meta-regression can be used to perform variable selection, retaining only the relevant moderators (Van Lissa, 2020; Van Lissa, van Erp, & Clapper, 2023).
text.formatted: And finally, if we suspect that there are systematic sources of heterogeneity, but we don't know which moderator variables are relevant, machine learning methods meta-regression can be used to perform variable selection, retaining only the relevant moderators <ref type="bibr">(Van Lissa, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Van Lissa, van Erp, & Clapper, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These methods address situations where there is no heterogeneity, random heterogeneity, or heterogeneity due to known and measured moderators.
A scenario that has been less commonly discussed occurs when there is systematic heterogeneity in effect sizes, but its causes are unmeasured, or not uniquely identifiable.
When this occurs, observed effect sizes do not follow a single normal distribution, but rather, a mixture of multiple normal distributions, as illustrated in Figure 1.
text.formatted: When this occurs, observed effect sizes do not follow a single normal distribution, but rather, a mixture of multiple normal distributions, as illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: The family of methods known by the umbrella term "Latent Class Analysis" (Vermunt et al., 2004) disentangles the underlying constituent distributions.
text.formatted: The family of methods known by the umbrella term "Latent Class Analysis" <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Vermunt et al., 2004)</ref> disentangles the underlying constituent distributions.

text.text: The finite normal mixture model -or latent profile analysis -assumes that each class is best described by a normal distribution, which renders it suitable for the analysis of continuous observed indicators, such as effect sizes in meta-analysis.
A mixture model assumes a known number of unobserved subgroups, called classes.
Like individual normal distributions, each class is characterized by two parameters: a mean and variance.
These can also be assumed to be equal across classes.
The model jointly estimates these class parameters, as well as the mixing proportions of the classes (how prevalent each class is).
The logic behind mixture modeling can be straightforwardly applied to meta-analysis.

One important difference from primary data analysis is that each observed datapoint is more or less informative about the mixture distributions, depending on its precision, which is determined by its sampling variance.
Studies with smaller sampling variance (typically those with larger samples) provide more accurate information about the (mixture) distribution of true effects.
For this reason, models for meta-analysis typically include a form of weightingeither explicitly, or implicitly via the model's likelihood -that accounts study-specific sampling variance.
The present study introduces a random-effects mixture -or "remix" -model for meta-analysis and evaluates its performance in a comprehensive simulation study.
The algorithm is implemented in the metamixture package, written in the free open source language R (R Core Team, 2026).
It builds upon the structural equation modeling framework of OpenMx (Boker et al., 2011).

text.text: To illustrate the relevance of the remix model for meta-analysis, we first present several scenarios where the model would be an appropriate choice.
The random-effects model is most commonly used for meta-analysis (Hedges & Vevea, 1998).

text.text: It assumes that between-study differences are normally distributed.
Let's consider several scenarios that would violate this assumption.
First, even if true effects are normally distributed in the population, the studies included in a meta-analysis may not constitute a representative sample of that population.
New studies are not designed to randomly probe the full range of conditions under which an effect could occur, but instead, they follow in the footsteps of work that has been done before.

Consequently, it may be more reasonable to think of published studies as a "snowball sample" from the population of possible studies, arising from a genetic process: each published study has a probability of inspiring further research, and this probability may be higher for studies with large effects than studies with small effects.

This follow-up research inherits will inherit many of the characteristics of the preceding work, and thus, new effect sizes are correlated with prior effect sizes, as are the values of any moderator variables that encode between-study differences.
The published effect sizes may thus contain an over-representation of specific populations, interventions, or measures.
It is easy to see how such a process would give rise to systematic deviations from normality in the distribution of published effect sizes.

For example, consider a field that is dominated by two strong "research traditions": A and B. Both favor a particular research design (e.g., experience sampling versus lab experiments), methodology (e.g., random prompts sent to participants' mobile devices, versus a series of computerized tasks), set of measures (questionnaire versus behavioral measures), and population (general public versus undergraduate students).
Within each tradition, there can be minor variations in all of these characteristics.

text.text: random-effects meta-analysis of all effect sizes would yield an unrepresentative pooled effect size: the average effect is exactly in the middle of both research traditions, and thus representative of neither.
Moverover, the estimated residual heterogeneity would be positively biased (inflated) by the differences between the two research traditions.
Even if the researcher had coded these moderators, they might still be practically prevented from accounting for them.
This moderator matrix has high multicolinearity: there is near-perfect overlap between the values of different moderators.

Including multicolinear moderators in a meta-regression makes it difficult to estimate each moderator's unique effect on effect size, resulting in unstable coefficient estimates, inflated standard errors, and poorly interpretable results (Steel & Kammeyer-Mueller, 2002).

As a second thought experiment, consider the presence of outliers in a meta-analytic dataset.
For example, imagine that a scholar has, for many years, asked undergraduate students to conduct pilot studies of a particular effect.
These pilot studies have small sample sizes, and thus show substantial variability in effect sizes.
Then, the researcher obtains funding to conduct a series of sufficiently powered experiments.
Not wanting students' work to go to waste, the researcher publishes a meta-analysis of all studies.
The distribution of scientific (publication) culture, and give readers cause to question the widely held assumption that effect sizes are always normally distributed.
Each scenario gives a reason for why, sometimes, one random-effects distribution is not enough.
In these cases and others, mixture models can be used to disentangle multiple underlying random-effects distributions.
For example, 1A calls for a two-class mixture model with free means and equal variances.
This allows us to tease apart the unique pooled effect sizes of the two research traditions.
Of course -an expert might assign each study to one tradition, and treat "assigned tradition" as a moderating variable.
However, this approach ignores measurement error in the coding of assigned tradition.
Note that the traditions are not perfectly distinct, and that some studies share similarities with both traditions.

A mixture model is a more elegant solution, as it allows each case to contribute to the estimation of both distributionsand thus, ambiguous studies that resemble both traditions will contribute to both distributions.
This also resolves the aforementioned multicolinearity problem.

The present study is emphatically not the first to introduce mixture models in meta-analysis.
Prior work has demonstrated their usefulness for addressing several methodological challenges.
One such application is the use of mixture models for moderator analysis.
Different approaches have been taken; for example, some authors have used mixture models to dichotomize the moderator matrix, and use predicted class membership in meta-regression (Graefe, 2025).

We introduce an open-source implementation of univariate random-effects mixture meta-analysis that accommodates class-specific or constrained mean effects and residual heterogeneity, while accounting for study-specific sampling variances.
It is implemented in the remix() function in the metamixture R-package.

Building on OpenMx, this implementation allows further model customization and extension, auxiliary analysis of predictors and moderators of class membership, and use of existing tools for reporting and visualization, like tidySEM.
We evaluate the performance of these models in a simulation study, focusing on parameter recovery, confidence interval (CI) coverage, and the identification of the number of latent classes.
Finite mixture models represent the observed data distribution as a mixture of multiple underlying distributions.
Each observation has a probability of belonging to one of k latent classes; the term "finite" implies that the number of components is known or fixed.
Each class, in turn, is defined by several parameters.
For a single observed continuous variable, these are often means µ 1...k and variances σ 2 1...k .
The overall distribution is a mixture of the class distributions, and each class contributes to the extent determined by the mixing proportion π k .
A class with a high mixing proportion contributes more to the overall distribution than one with a low mixing proportion.
Unlike mixture models for individual participant data, random-effects mixture models must account for sampling variance.
In the conventional random effects model, the observed sampling variance is treated as known to construct a weighted likelihood.

Two well-established approaches to class enumeration are information theoretical methods and likelihood ratio tests.
Information theoretical methods select the model with the lowest value on a statistic that balances model fit and complexity, by adding a complexity penalty to the minus two log-likelihood.

Examples include the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC, Akaike, 1974), Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC, Schwarz, 1978), or Integrated Completed Likelihood (Biernacki, Celeux, & Govaert, 2000), where the latter is unique in penalizing poor class separation as well.

text.text: In cross-validation, observed effect sizes are randomly split into multiple subsets.
Each candidate model is fitted on effect sizes from all subsets except one, and the fitted model's predictive performance is evaluated on the one held-out subset.

To circumvent this problem, we instead used the aforementioned surprisal statistic to evaluate how surprising the held-out effect sizes are in the estimated mixture distribution.
A key distinction is that the likelihood of the held-out effect sizes can be directly evaluated with respect to the cross-validated model's parameters, rather then the simulated data density.
Surprisal scores are summed across subsets.
The model with the lowest value has the best out-of-sample predictive performance, and is selected.

Given a trade-off between overfitting and underfitting, the latter is preferable for mixture models, whose parameter counts rapidly increases with the number of classes, which can lead to empirical under-identification when samples are small (Van Lissa et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Given a trade-off between overfitting and underfitting, the latter is preferable for mixture models, whose parameter counts rapidly increases with the number of classes, which can lead to empirical under-identification when samples are small <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Van Lissa et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, here, parsimony clearly comes at the cost of inaccuracy.
AIC and BIC performed best, followed by PMC and CV.
ICL performed at near-chance levels.
Compared to AIC and BIC, PMC and CV have the advantage of offering class enumeration tests, but this comes at the expense of a loss of performance.
These findings suggest that, even when mixture parameters can be estimated with reasonable accuracy, reliably identifying the underlying number of latent classes remains difficult.
Study 2 demonstrated that remix offers a computationally efficient and competitive alternative to the existing metaplus package.
Both algorithms mostly found the same solutions; when their solutions differed, remix most often found the better solution.
Importantly, while the algorithms had comparable performance in terms of parameter estimation accuracy, remix was much faster to run (22 times).

CI coverage of both methods was comparable for the pooled effect sizes, but could not be compared for residual heterogeneity and mixing proportions because metaplus did not provide confidence intervals for these parameters.
Taken together, results from these two studies indicate that remix reliably estimates the parameters of random-effects mixture meta-analysis.
Moreover, remix performs similarly to metaplus for special cases covered by both implementations.
However, statistical inference and reliable class enumeration remain challenging, particularly with small samples and poor class separation.

A strength of the present study is that it introduces the remix method for estimating random-effects mixture models, whose class means and heterogeneity parameters can be freely estimated, constrained to be equal, or fixed at specific values.
This model is more general than those considered in previous research.

We implemented this method in the remix() function of the metamixture package: a user-friendly wrapper with similar interface to existing functions like metafor::rma(yi, vi) for random-effects meta-analysis (Viechtbauer, 2010) and tidySEM::mx_profiles() (Van Lissa et al., 2024) for mixture models.
text.formatted: We implemented this method in the remix() function of the metamixture package: a user-friendly wrapper with similar interface to existing functions like metafor::rma(yi, vi) for random-effects meta-analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Viechtbauer, 2010)</ref> and tidySEM::mx_profiles() <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Van Lissa et al., 2024)</ref> for mixture models.

text.text: The backend in OpenMx ensures efficient and fast estimation.

Furthermore, it is a general-purpose structural equation modeling framework, which means models can be fully customized (e.g., with equality constraints, starting values, auxiliary variable analyses) within its broader structural equation modeling framework.
Information-based standard errors and profile-likelihood confidence intervals are available out of the box in OpenMx, and the estimated models interface with many other packages.
Prior research has discussed mixture meta-analysis in the context of moderator analysis (Graefe, 2025; Zhang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Prior research has discussed mixture meta-analysis in the context of moderator analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Graefe, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Zhang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: With the tidySEM R-package, it is straightforward to conduct such moderator analyses with class as a predictor, or to predict class membership as an outcome, or even to conduct auxiliary analyses with a structural equation model of arbitrary complexity with class as a grouping variable.
When examining class as a predictor of distal outcomes or moderator of auxiliary models, one option is to use the BCH approach (Bolck et al., 2004).
text.formatted: When examining class as a predictor of distal outcomes or moderator of auxiliary models, one option is to use the BCH approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bolck et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: It estimates a multi-group structural equation model using assigned class as grouping variable, accounting for classification error by weighting individual cases' contributions.
A downside of BCH is that its standard errors are not valid.
When valid standard errors are required, the two-step approach is a suitable alternative (two_step()).

This method first estimates the latent class model, then freezes its parameters and adds the auxiliary structural equation model so that the latter doesn't influence the estimation of the class solution (Bakk & Kuha, 2018).
text.formatted: This method first estimates the latent class model, then freezes its parameters and adds the auxiliary structural equation model so that the latter doesn't influence the estimation of the class solution <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bakk & Kuha, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In principle, both BCH and the two-step method can be used to identify significant predictors of class membership, but only in the univariate case.
To this end, the candidate predictor is specified as an auxiliary variable.
Based on an assumption of causal directionality, a significant omnibus test for between-class differences in the predictor is interpreted as evidence that it predicts class membership.
A more flexible approach that can explicitly treat class membership as either a predictor an outcome is the pseudo-class method (Wang et al., 2005).
text.formatted: A more flexible approach that can explicitly treat class membership as either a predictor an outcome is the pseudo-class method <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Wang et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: It repeatedly draws random samples of class membership based on the individual posterior class probabilities, estimates the auxiliary model for each random sample, and then integrates the results across samples to account for classification uncertainty.
All of these functions are implemented in tidySEM, along with functions for plotting and tabulating results (Van Lissa et al., 2024).
text.formatted: All of these functions are implemented in tidySEM, along with functions for plotting and tabulating results <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Van Lissa et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A key limitation of the method is that its CI coverage is low.
This is a known limitation of mixture models, particularly with small sample sizes and model misspecification (Nylund, Asparouhov, & Muthén, 2007).
text.formatted: This is a known limitation of mixture models, particularly with small sample sizes and model misspecification <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Nylund, Asparouhov, & Muthén, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Small samples are common in meta-analysis, and indeed, most sample sizes in our simulation study were below the minimum size that has been considered in studies on regular mixture models.
Poor class separability may be a contributing cause of poor CI coverage in mixture models in general.
For mixture meta-analysis in particular, the additional heterogeneity introduced by sampling variance might further diminish coverage.
This interpretation is bolstered by prior work that reported poor CI coverage for (different versions of) mixture meta-analysis (Beath, 2014; Negeri, 2025).
text.formatted: This interpretation is bolstered by prior work that reported poor CI coverage for (different versions of) mixture meta-analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Beath, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Negeri, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Further research into the causes of poor CI coverage in mixture models is needed.
Another limitation is the poor performance of all class enumeration methods.
This lack of power for class enumeration has been reported in previous work, especially for imperfect class separation (Tein, Coxe, & Cham, 2013).
text.formatted: This lack of power for class enumeration has been reported in previous work, especially for imperfect class separation <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Tein, Coxe, & Cham, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: While we investigated conditions ranging from poor to very good class separation, performance of all class enumeration methods was subpar across conditions.
While it is possible that some methods would perform better when classes are perfectly separated, we focused on investigating more realistic scenarios where class membership is somewhat ambiguous.
Further research specifically focused on class enumeration methods could investigate conditions under which different class enumeration methods perform well.
One further limitation is that our simulation study focused on normal population distributions.

When true effects follow skewed, heavy-tailed, or other non-normal distributions, class performance may deteriorate, as classes attempt to capture distributional idiosyncrasies (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2016).
text.formatted: When true effects follow skewed, heavy-tailed, or other non-normal distributions, class performance may deteriorate, as classes attempt to capture distributional idiosyncrasies <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Asparouhov & Muthén, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Future research could examine alternative within-class distributions.
The models presented here assume independent effect sizes, but commonly, multiple effect sizes are extracted from each paper, yielding a nested data structure.
Future approaches might examine extensions of the method presented here to dependent effect sizes or multilevel data structures.

The most straightforward approach would be to include all effect sizes in model estimation, ignoring the dependent structure, and then computing consistent standard errors for inference, using the sandwich estimator (Yuan, 2016).
text.formatted: The most straightforward approach would be to include all effect sizes in model estimation, ignoring the dependent structure, and then computing consistent standard errors for inference, using the sandwich estimator <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Yuan, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This is implemented as an ad-hoc solution in sandwich_remix(), but further research on its performance is needed.
An alternative approach is to perform clustered bootstrapping, which is trivial to implement using R's replicate() function, but computationally expensive.
Recommendations for applied researchers.
For general recommendations regarding mixture modeling, we refer readers to Van Lissa et al. (2024).
text.formatted: For general recommendations regarding mixture modeling, we refer readers to <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Van Lissa et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: Based on the present study, we provide several additional recommendations regarding random-effects mixture models in particular.
These models can be reliably estimated, even with relatively small samples; they have low parameter bias on average and reasonably good CI coverage, albeit below nominal levels.

Because all class enumeration methods performed poorly, random-effects mixture meta-analysis is not very suitable for exploratory analysis, where the number of classes is unknown (Van Lissa et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Because all class enumeration methods performed poorly, random-effects mixture meta-analysis is not very suitable for exploratory analysis, where the number of classes is unknown <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Van Lissa et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As all class enumeration methods tended to underfit, there is little risk of inadvertently selecting an overly complex solution.
However, failure to identify additional classes should not be interpreted as evidence of absence of distinct subpopulations.
The primary use case for random-effects mixture meta-analysis is confirmatory analysis, where distinct subpopulations of true effects are expected based on a theoretical rationale.
As explained in the introduction, such subpopulations could arise from different research traditions, intervention types, or study populations.
Practices like p-hacking and publication bias, or the presence of outliers, may also produce distinct components in the observed effect-size distribution.
Mixture models can capture these distinct sources of heterogeneity that would otherwise be obscured in a conventional random-effects model.
Researchers should be aware of the limitations associated with small samples, which are prevalent in meta-analyses.
There is no rule of thumb for minimum sample size, as the information available for estimating a mixture model also depends on class proportions, separation, and within-class heterogeneity.
In our simulation studies, the remix method performed acceptably with as few as 20 observations and moderate class separation.
In general, small samples cause greater parameter bias, lower CI coverage, and poorer class enumeration performance.
Pragmatically, researchers might favor parsimonious models (e.g., 2 classes), because small samples might not provide enough information to reliably estimate a higher number of classes.
When drawing conclusions, researchers should exercise caution in generalizing from the sample to the population of all possible effect sizes.

The safest approach is to consider the results of small sample meta-analysis as descriptive of the published effect sizes in a field, but not necessarily representative of its population distribution.
Researchers should always evaluate model convergence and the stability of the estimated solution.
Mixture likelihoods can contain multiple local optima, and successful numerical optimization does not guarantee that the global maximum has been identified.

Although remix() uses simulated annealing and falls back on multiple random starts when the model fails to converge, researchers should inspect convergence diagnostics using tidySEM::mx_convergence(), and consider using random_starts() with a high number of nstarts to assess whether a better global optimum exists.

Particular caution is warranted when one class has a very small proportion, when heterogeneity estimates approach their boundaries (e.g., due to a single outlier), or when parameter estimates change substantially across optimization attempts.
When performing auxiliary analyses (predicting class membership or testing for class differences in some outcome), always account for classification uncertainty.
Simply assigning studies to their most likely class and treating these assignments as known biases these auxiliary analyses.
The tidySEM package offers several approaches that account for classification uncertainty (BCH(), two_step(), and pseudo_class()).
The two-step approach is particularly useful for predicting distal outcomes (or auxiliary models) from class membership, as it produces corrected standard errors.
The pseudo-class method is most flexible when class membership can be either a predictor or an outcome.
There are many common scenarios in meta-analysis where heterogeneity is expected, for example, as a result of different research traditions, questionable research practices, or publication bias.
In such cases, random-effects mixture meta-analysis is a useful technique to investigate unobserved sources of heterogeneity.

The present study introduced and evaluated a generalized approach to random-effects mixture modeling that accounts for known sampling variances while allowing class means and heterogeneity parameters to be either freely estimated, constrained across classes, or fixed to known values.

The remix() implementation, with a back-end in OpenMx, facilitates user-friendly model specification and customization, offers out-of-the box efficient estimation and information-and likelihood-based inference.

The estimated models are compatible with other R-packages in the OpenMx ecosystem, like tidySEM, which can be used for valid analysis of predictors and outcomes of class membership, as well as reporting results in a publication-ready manner.
Two simulation studies showed that remix() performs well, and on par with existing solutions.
Parameter recovery was unbiased on average and CI coverage was reasonable but below nominal levels.
However, class enumeration methods performed poorly.

These findings suggest that random-effects mixture meta-analysis is a useful method for explaining heterogeneity in effect sizes, especially when the number of classes is known based on theoretical or substantive considerations.
